# 🧭 What Is Quarto? {#what-is-quarto}

[⏱️ 0:10]{.clock}

## Quarto = Markdown → Anything {#quarto-hub}

![](assets/quarto-hub.svg){fig-alt="Two inputs, a .md Markdown file and a .qmd file with code in Python, R, bash, SQL, MATLAB, Java, JavaScript or C, flow into Quarto, shown by its four-quadrant logo, which combines Pandoc with Jupyter and knitr. Quarto produces four groups of formats: documents (html, pdf, docx, odt and, highlighted, epub); presentations (revealjs, pptx, beamer); the web (website, blog, dashboard); and more (Markdown, Jupyter notebooks, JATS, wikis)." width="74%" fig-align="center"}

🆓 **Free and open source** · no licence to buy, for anyone · [MIT License](https://quarto.org/license.html)

[📚 [All Quarto output formats](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html) ·
Quarto logo: Posit, PBC]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Say this early: Quarto costs nothing and needs no licence key, for individuals, universities and
companies alike. The Quarto CLI is under the MIT License from version 1.4 (GNU GPL v2 before that),
and the tools it bundles have their own open-source licences
(https://quarto.org/license.html, checked 2026-11-06). The paid part of today is the coding
assistant, a separate tool: the next slides come back to that. Pandoc converts the Markdown. Code cells run in Jupyter (Python) or knitr (R), and their
results are inserted. Quarto's principal languages are Python, R, Julia and Observable
JavaScript (`{ojs}` cells, run in the reader's browser); Jupyter kernels add many more,
such as MATLAB or Java (https://quarto.org/docs/faq/,
https://quarto.org/docs/computations/ojs.html). knitr's engines run `{sql}`, `{c}` and
`{bash}` cells (https://pkg.yihui.org/rmarkdown-book/language-engines.html); in Jupyter,
`!` lines run shell commands
(https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#shell-commands). Today we
use Python only. The official
list groups documents (HTML, PDF, MS Word, OpenDocument, ePub), presentations (Revealjs,
PowerPoint, Beamer), Markdown flavours, wikis and more (Jupyter, JATS, RTF, …):
https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html. ePub is the e-book format:
https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/epub.html. Websites and blogs
(https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) and dashboards (https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/)
are built from the same files. All checked 2026-10-30. The Quarto logo is a Posit, PBC
trademark, used here to refer to Quarto (https://quarto.org/trademark.html).
:::

## 🚫🤖 Quarto Is Not AI {#quarto-not-ai}

::: {.cards}
::: {}
[⚙️]{.big}

**Traditional software**

same input → same output, every time
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📚]{.big}

**Built for publishing**

quality documents, slides and websites
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🤖]{.big}

**The assistant is separate**

it writes the files · Quarto turns them into formats
:::
:::

. . .

🔁 No AI inside Quarto: it follows your source exactly

::: {.notes}
Participants sometimes assume Quarto is an AI tool because the workshop uses a coding
assistant. It is not: Quarto is open-source publishing software (built on Pandoc, with
Jupyter or knitr running code) that reads Markdown and code and writes the same outputs
every time for the same inputs and data. It does not generate text, code or figures by
itself and sends nothing to an AI service. The coding assistant is a separate tool that
writes and edits the source files on request; Quarto then renders them. That split matters
for trust: the assistant can make mistakes, so you check its files, while a render is
repeatable. Code cells you add run whatever code they contain, so if a cell calls an AI
service, that is your code, not Quarto. See https://quarto.org/ (not yet re-checked for
this slide).
:::

## 🔁 Reproducible: Same Source, Same Result {#reproducible}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[📄]{.big}

**One source**

text + code + data in plain files
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🧮]{.big}

**Numbers are computed**

never typed or pasted in
:::
::: {.fragment}
[▶️]{.big}

**One command**

`quarto render` rebuilds everything
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🕰️]{.big}

**Versioned with git**

every change saved · `uv.lock` pins the tools
:::
:::

. . .

✏️ Change one value in the data → render → **table, chart and sentence all update**

🏷️ `git` (set up next) records which version of the files produced which result

::: {.check}
💬 You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?
:::

::: {.notes}
Reproducible means that someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results
from the same files with one command, and that you can see where every number came from. It
is the reason for the workshop's structure. The report is source, not a pasted result: its
figures, tables and numbers in sentences are computed by code cells and inline code from
the data files, so changing an input and re-rendering updates every output without
retyping (the "change an input, rebuild, and explain what updated" outcome). Reproducibility
depends on versioning: git, the version control tool installed in Setup, saves a numbered
snapshot (a commit) of the source, data and settings together with a message saying what
changed and why. Any earlier snapshot can be restored, two versions compared, and a result
tied to the exact files that made it; without versions, "the same source" is whatever
happens to be on the disk today. GitHub then keeps a shared copy, and the same history
backs the AI usage statement: you can show what the assistant changed and what you
reviewed. The project's `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` are versioned too: they pin the
Python packages, so a participant's machine and a colleague's give the same environment. This matters most with a coding assistant: it may
write code that looks right and is not, so we ask it to compute from the data and then
render and check, and anyone can re-run the render to confirm. Reproducible does not mean
correct: a wrong analysis reproduces perfectly, so we still check results against their
sources. Good answer to the check: nothing; fix the data and re-render.
:::

## 📶 You Need a Stable, Fast Internet Connection {#internet}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[⬇️]{.big}

**Big downloads**

Ubuntu, Quarto, the assistant, Python packages, data
:::
::: {.fragment}
[☁️]{.big}

**The assistant is online**

every reply needs the connection · it stops when the Wi-Fi drops
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🏠]{.big}

**Do setup at home**

wired or strong Wi-Fi · avoid hotels, trains, firewalled work networks
:::
:::

. . .

🔌 Plugged in · 📵 No VPN or proxy if you can · 🧪 Test run done at home = ready

::: {.notes}
Almost every setup step downloads something: the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes),
Quarto, uv and the Python packages, the assistant itself, and the workshop data. The coding
assistant also sends every request to a model over the internet, so a poor connection shows
up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which participants often take for
their own mistakes. Ask everyone to do the setup on a reliable connection, and to bring a
phone hotspot as a fallback. Company networks with a proxy or TLS inspection often block
downloads: raise it before the day. In the room, check that the venue Wi-Fi copes with every
participant downloading at once, and say what to do if it does not.
:::

## 🆘 Error? Ask an AI Chat {#ask-ai-chat}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [🆘 when stuck]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[📋]{.big}

**Copy**

the command you ran + the **full** error text
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🌐]{.big}

**Paste into a web chat**

Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT in your browser, with your system (Windows + Ubuntu, or Mac)
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔧]{.big}

**Try the fix**

one suggestion at a time · read it before you run it
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔁]{.big}

**Still failing?**

paste the new error · then Discord `#help`
:::
:::

. . .

🔒 No passwords, keys or private data in the paste

::: {.notes}
Installs fail before the coding assistant works, and sometimes the assistant itself is what
fails, so the participant needs a second route that does not depend on it: a free web chat in
the browser (Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT). Good habits: paste the exact command and the whole
error, say the operating system (for WSL: Windows with Ubuntu on WSL), say what step of the
deck you are on, and try one suggested fix at a time. Read each command before running it:
a chat can be wrong, and never run a command that deletes things or asks for
administrator rights without understanding why. Remove passwords, tokens, API keys and
private data first (the AI-policy slide later explains why). If two suggestions fail, post the error and
what you tried in Discord. This is the same habit the workshop teaches with the assistant:
you direct, check and take responsibility. The room rule remains: two minutes stuck, ask.
:::

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [💬 get help]{.pace}

::: {.notes}
Discord is where the organiser and participants talk during the workshop: questions, error
screenshots and links go in the text channels, and the voice channels are for the group and
for pairing. Send the invite link with the pre-work, and ask people to join before the day
so that problems with accounts or the app show up early. A server is the whole workshop
space; it holds channels. Text channels are named with a `#`, voice channels have a speaker
icon. Discord runs in the browser, as a desktop app and on a phone. Also useful: reply to a
message to answer it, add a reaction to say "seen" without noise, and mute channels you do
not need. When someone is stuck, ask for the exact command, the full error text and a
screenshot, and remember the room rule: two minutes stuck, then catch up. The organiser
supplies the real invite link and channel names for each run; this deck does not publish
a link.

## 🔁 Discord ↔ WhatsApp {#discord-whatsapp}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [💬 get help]{.pace}

| 💬 Discord | 📱 WhatsApp |
|---|---|
| Server | Community |
| Text channel | Group chat |
| Voice channel | Group call you can join and leave |
| `@name` tag | `@name` mention |
| Reply to a message | Reply to a message |
| Direct message | Chat with one person |
| Invite link | Group invite link |
| Reaction | Reaction |

. . .

⚠️ Unlike a WhatsApp group, a Discord server has **many channels**: pick the right one

::: {.notes}
Use this for participants who know WhatsApp but not Discord. The mapping is approximate: a
server is closest to a WhatsApp Community, which also holds several groups, and a text channel
is closest to one group chat. A voice channel is always open: you join to talk and leave when
done, with no call to start or answer. Discord also has threads (a side conversation under
one message) and roles, which have no close WhatsApp equivalent. WhatsApp features and names
change, so check the right-hand column against the app before teaching.
:::

::: {}
**🍎 Mac**
:::

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

::: {}
**🐧 Ubuntu, Debian**
:::

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
```
:::

::: {.hint}
🪟 9 short steps · 🛡️ admin account · 🔁 one restart: 📱 open it on your phone too

🍎 ⌘ Space, type `Terminal`, Enter · paste · click **Install** · wait

🐧 Ctrl+Alt+T · password stays hidden · other Linux: install `curl` and `git` your usual way
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 20 min

::: {.done}
`git --version` prints a version. 🪟 In Ubuntu, and `wsl -l -v` shows VERSION 2.
:::

::: {.notes}
Every system gets ready here, so nobody skips step 1. The commands install `git` and `curl`, which
the next steps assume. Windows is the big one, and participants found it the hardest at the
workshop of 2026-11-05. It lives on its own page, `windows-setup.qmd`, because a beginner needs one
action at a time and a "you should see" after each, in a page that scrolls, can be kept beside
the terminal, survives the restart on a phone, and is translated by the browser. The page opens
with the picture of Windows as a house and Ubuntu as a room inside it, then covers the WSL install
in an administrator PowerShell, the restart, the same command again in a normal window (distributions
are per user, so someone else's administrator password must not install it), the first Ubuntu
start, the `wsl -l -v` check, copy and paste, `sudo apt install curl git`, four habits, and the
stuck-table. The command runs twice because on current WSL, when a restart is needed, `wsl
--install` only enables Windows features and installs no distribution
(https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/blob/3.0.3/src/windows/common/WslClient.cpp#L557-L564, checked
2026-11-06). `--no-launch` keeps first-time setup out of the administrator PowerShell tab, whose
folder would be `/mnt/c/WINDOWS/system32`; the Start menu's Ubuntu opens in `~`. Without
administrator rights or BIOS access WSL cannot be installed: collect such participants before the
day and pair them with a neighbour (no native Windows route is supported).

On a Mac, the first `git` opens a dialog to install Apple's Command Line Tools
(https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-Installing-Git), so left alone it interrupts the
assistant's install at step 4. `xcode-select --install` makes that a deliberate step at home
(https://docs.brew.sh/Installation, which also says Homebrew needs these tools only to build from
source). Quarto's Mac download is a standalone `.pkg` (https://quarto.org/docs/download/). All
checked 2026-11-06. Apple's own page could not be read by the check, and the dialog's wording
and download time are not documented here. "Already installed" from that command is fine: go
on. `sudo` asks for the Linux password, which stays hidden as you type. On other Linux, install
`curl` and `git` with its package manager. Written from documentation and not yet tried on a clean Mac or a Windows machine:
run both once before teaching.
:::

## 📁 Move Around the Terminal {#terminal-basics}

### Exercise · ⏱️ 4 min

::: {.done}
you typed these, and after `cd ~` the prompt shows `~` again. Then `rmdir demo/notes demo`.
:::
:::
::::

[👀 Just watch this one, then type the bold words yourself, with Enter after each · `~` = your home folder · 🍎 Mac: `ana@mac ~ %`, only the last folder (`ana@mac notes %`) and `/Users/ana`]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Everyone, on every system: the rest of the workshop happens in a terminal, a window where you
type commands instead of clicking. The picture is Ubuntu on Windows (WSL) in Windows Terminal,
where Windows 11 opens 🪟 Start → Ubuntu; Windows 10's plainer window, a Mac or a Linux terminal
look different but answer the same.
The terminal opens in your home folder, written `~` (here `/home/ana`; on a Mac `/Users/ana`).
`pwd` prints the current folder, `date` the day and time (`-05` is the time zone, as in
Colombia), `ls` lists the folder (Ubuntu shows folders in blue), `mkdir name` creates a folder,
`cd name` enters it, `cd ..` goes up one level and `cd ~` (or `cd` alone) goes straight home
from anywhere. The bold words are what you type. The part up to `$`, the prompt, is the terminal
saying who and where you are and that it is ready: `ana` is the Linux user, `LAPTOP-4K7Q2PM` the
Windows computer's name (yours differs), and the folder after the colon changes with every `cd`:
`~/demo`, `~/demo/notes`, back to `~/demo`, then `~`. The other lines are the answers. The
example is a picture of a session, so it cannot be selected or copied: typing it is the
exercise. On a Mac the prompt is `ana@mac ~ %`, ending in `%`, not `$`: same meaning; it shows
only the last folder, with no colon (`ana@mac demo %`, `ana@mac notes %`), and `pwd` gives the
full path. Tab
completes names, and the up arrow recalls the previous command: both save typing mistakes, so
show them. Type these rather than pasting them: the hands remember. Later slides ask you to run
`mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide`: this is that (`-p` makes no fuss if the folder
exists, `&&` means "and then, if that worked"). Ask while they type: after `cd ..`, what would
`pwd` print? Good answer: `/home/ana/demo`. Do the exercise from the home folder, where the
terminal opens; `rmdir demo/notes demo` at the end removes both empty folders, inner one first,
so the exercise can be repeated.
:::

## 🧩 Install a Coding Assistant {#install-assistant}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [🧭 Step 3/6]{.pace} [🪟 in Ubuntu · 🍎 `claude` not found? Paste the fix it printed, then a new tab]{.pillnote}

::: {.you .installers}
::: {}
**✳️ Claude Code** · [setup](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup)
:::

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
```

::: {}
**🌀 Codex** · [guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli)
:::

```bash
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
```

::: {}
**♊ Antigravity** · [docs](https://antigravity.google/docs/getting-started?tab=cli)
:::

```bash
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
```
:::

::: {.hint}
1️⃣ **Pick one:** paste its line, press Enter · 2️⃣ **New tab:** 🪟 Ctrl+Shift+D · 🍎 ⌘T · 🐧 Ctrl+Shift+T

3️⃣ **Start it:** `mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup`, then `claude`, `codex` or `agy` · trust this folder? ↓ to Yes, then Enter ([👀 screens](#assistant-screens))

4️⃣ **Sign in:** no browser? Copy the link it prints, whole, into yours · a code appears? Paste it back here
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 5 min

::: {.done}
the assistant answers when you type `hello`. Then type `/exit`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do this before the workshop. `curl ... | bash` downloads the vendor's small install script and
runs it: only do this with links you trust, here each vendor's own documented command. A new
tab is needed because a terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so it cannot find
one installed a moment ago; that is the usual `command not found` straight after an install. On
a Mac a new tab is not enough for Claude Code: its installer leaves `~/.local/bin` off the PATH
and prints the fix under "Setup notes" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/troubleshoot-install,
checked 2026-11-06). Starting in `~/setup` means the first "trust this folder?" answer is safe;
📂 Your Root Folder, in 📖 Read Before the Day, explains why. Sign-in without a browser, as in WSL, ends with a code to paste back
at `Paste code here`; if pasting does nothing, right-click or Shift+Insert (same page).
Sign in with an account that has access to the tool: Claude
Code needs a Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup),
Codex a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth), Antigravity a
Google account. WSL cannot open a browser: Claude Code and Antigravity print a URL, which you
copy into the Windows browser, then paste the code back; if Codex's browser sign-in fails,
`codex login --device-auth` (first enable device codes in ChatGPT security settings).
Sign-up and email verification can take hours, so do not leave them for the day. Account
and sign-in details checked 2026-11-03; they change often, so re-check them before teaching.
Claude Code installer: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup. Codex standalone installer
for macOS and Linux: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli, which also lists Windows,
`npm install -g @openai/codex` and Homebrew. Google's Antigravity CLI (`agy`):
https://antigravity.google/docs/getting-started?tab=cli, which also lists PowerShell and
CMD installers for Windows. It replaced Gemini CLI for unpaid-tier and Google One users on
18 June 2026 (https://www.geminicli.com/docs/get-started/installation); existing Gemini CLI
settings are migrated on first launch (https://antigravity.google/docs/cli/gcli-migration/).
All checked 2026-10-30. Start the assistant inside the exercise folder, and never run two
assistants writing to one folder.
:::

## ⌨️ Two Places to Type {#two-places}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 read before step 4]{.pace}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.you}
**🖥️ The terminal** · its line ends in `$` (🍎 `%`)

```{=html}
<div class="terminal mini" role="img" aria-label="A terminal prompt, with pwd typed after it."><pre translate="no"><span class="pr">ana@laptop:~/setup$</span> <b>pwd</b></pre></div>
```

commands: `pwd`, `cd`, `quarto preview`
:::
:::
::: {.column width="49%"}
::: {.prompt}
**🤖 The assistant** · it runs inside the terminal

`> Which tools are missing?`

plain language, and `/` commands: `/exit`
:::
:::
::::

. . .

🚪 **In:** type `claude` · **Out:** type `/exit` · box colours say which place

::: {.hint}
➕ Assistant busy and a green box to do? Second tab: 🪟 Ctrl+Shift+D · 🍎 ⌘T · 🐧 Ctrl+Shift+T

😌 Wrong place? Usually harmless: `command not found`, or the assistant just reads it
:::

::: {.check}
💬 The assistant is running and a slide says to type `gh auth login`. Where do you type it?
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the mix-up that costs beginners the most time, so it gets its own slide before the
first prompt. The assistant takes over the terminal tab while it runs: what you type goes to
it, not to the shell, until `/exit`. Green "You type" boxes go in the terminal; violet "Ask
your coding assistant" boxes go in the assistant. The same colours mark every hands-on slide,
and the three-boxes slide returns to them in the room. A prompt typed at `$` usually gives
`command not found`, and a command typed into the assistant is usually read as a request, so
neither is a disaster: look at the line you are on and try again. On a Mac the terminal's
line ends in `%`. Good answer to the check: in a second terminal tab, because `gh auth login`
needs you and the assistant is using the first tab; `/exit` first also works, but ends the
conversation.
:::

## 🐧 The Assistant Installs the Tools {#install-tools}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [🧭 Step 4/6]{.pace} [🪟 in Ubuntu · 👋 `/exit` first · not Claude? `codex` or `agy`]{.pillnote}

::: {.you}
```bash
mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude
```
:::

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. Never run `sudo`, or an installer that asks for a password, yourself: print each such command alone in a code block, using full paths, then wait until I say done. Then print every version.
```
:::

::: {.hint}
👀 Read each command it asks about, then approve · 🔐 A command for you (`sudo` = administrator)? Paste it into a **second tab**, type your password (hidden), then type `done` here

🍎 Password = your Mac login · "Command line developer tools" pop-up? Click Install, wait, then type `done`
:::

### Exercise · ⏱️ 10 min

::: {.done}
it prints a version for all five tools. Then type `/exit`.
:::

::: {.notes}
The assistant now does what a block of install commands did before, so the slide holds one
prompt. `sudo` means "do this as administrator". Leaving with `/exit` matters: uv's and
Quarto's commands are only found by a terminal started after the install, and the next step
starts the assistant again from a new tab. It must be installed first (step 3). An assistant cannot type a password, so the prompt asks it to hand those
commands back, with full paths because a second tab starts in the home folder; the participant
pastes them in that tab, where `sudo` asks for the Linux password chosen at the first start
(typing shows nothing), then says `done`, so nobody has to copy hundreds of lines of `apt` output
back. On a clean Mac, the first use of `git` opens Apple's "command line developer tools" dialog,
and Homebrew's installer asks for the Mac login password. Behind the prompt the
assistant normally runs `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git`, uv's installer
(https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/, `~/.local/bin`, so only a new
shell sees it), the Quarto `.deb` from the GitHub release page (Quarto has no Ubuntu apt
package, https://quarto.org/docs/download/) and the GitHub CLI (Ubuntu's own `gh` package
is discouraged, https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md). On macOS it
uses Homebrew or the same official installers. Needs Quarto 1.10 or later. Behind a
corporate proxy the downloads can fail: tell the organiser before the day. Not yet tried
on a Windows machine with an assistant: run it once in a fresh Ubuntu before teaching.
:::

## 🛠️ Setup Check {#setup-check}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [🧭 Step 5/6]{.pace} [🪟 in Ubuntu · ➕ new tab first · not Claude? `codex` or `agy`]{.pillnote}

::: {.you}
```bash
cd ~/setup && claude
```
:::

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this assistant, and run `quarto check` (no Jupyter or LaTeX yet is fine: count it as OK). If `git config --global user.name` or `user.email` is unset, ask me for my name and my GitHub email, then set them. Clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git to `~/quarto-workshop` (if it exists, `git pull` only when its working tree is clean) and list its `checkpoints/`. Run `gh auth status`. Run every check even if one fails, then report each as OK or not.
```
:::

::: {.hint}

## 🧠 Model + 🔧 Harness = 🤖 Assistant {#model-harness}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);"}
::: {}
[🧠]{.big}

**Model**

reads and writes text, asks for tools
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔧]{.big}

**Harness**

files, commands, permissions
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🤖]{.big}

**Coding assistant**

model + harness in your terminal
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.bigline}
🧠 The model decides · 🔧 the harness does · 👀 you direct and check
:::

🔁 Many harnesses can run several models: same tool, different results

::: {.notes}
The model is the language model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini). The harness is the
program around it: it gives the model tools to read and write files, run commands and
search, asks you to approve actions, and feeds results back in a loop. The assistants on the
install slide (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) are harnesses; many can run several models, so
the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves
differently in a different harness. That is why the next slide is about choosing a model, and
why no model is always right: check its work (the "you direct and check" rule).
:::

## 📏 Main Models: Pick by Task {#model-choice}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace} [in each column: cheapest at the top]{.pillnote}

::: {.model-table}

| ✳️ Claude | Good for | 🌀 ChatGPT | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Haiku 5.5** ✅ [from \$]{.price} | simple, high-volume tasks | **GPT-6 Luna** [\$]{.price} | focused, high-volume tasks |
| **Sonnet 5.5** ✅ [\$\$\$]{.price} | daily coding: speed + intelligence | **GPT-6.1 Terra** [\$\$\$]{.price} | visual reasoning, computer use, clear writing |
| **Opus 5.5** [\$\$\$\$]{.price} | long-running coding and knowledge work | **GPT-6.1 Sol** ✅ [\$\$\$]{.price} | complex work, balancing intelligence and cost |
| **Fable 5.1** [\$\$\$\$\$]{.price} | demanding reasoning, long-horizon work | **GPT-6 Astra** [\$\$\$\$\$]{.price} | the most demanding work |

: {tbl-colwidths="[19,31,19,31]"}

:::

✅ **Enough today:** Haiku or Sonnet on **medium** · Sol on **low**

📉 Expect the same capability **100–1000×** cheaper

::: {.check}
💬 Which would you pick to fix a typo, and which to join two datasets?
:::

[each \$ ≈ 3× the API price per 1M tokens · uses paraphrased from the vendors' docs · rows are not equivalents · [Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview) · [ChatGPT](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models), checked 2026-11-06 · 📉 so far ≈ 10× or more a year: [a16z](https://a16z.com/llmflation-llm-inference-cost/) · [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends)]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Each company offers a family, from small and cheap to large and capable, and they do not all do the
same job: the table is about use cases, not a ranking. Larger, more recent models usually follow
longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from errors better, while small models are
quicker and cheaper and are often enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or
reformatting a table. Hard tasks here, such as joining datasets or debugging a failed render,
reward the stronger model. Good answer to the check: a small model for the typo, the strongest
available for the join. If a prompt keeps failing, try a stronger model inside your assistant (see
its documentation for how). For this workshop the prompts are short and well specified, so Haiku or
Sonnet with the effort (reasoning) setting on medium, or ChatGPT's Sol on low, is sufficient. Both
vendors give a stronger starting point for unknown, hard work: Anthropic says to start with Opus 5.5
for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. Our advice is
smaller because these prompts are small and it saves your credits.

Each column is in price order, and a row is not a pairing: there are no benchmarks here, Sol and
Sonnet cost the same, and Terra costs half as much inside the same \$\$\$ band. The \$ tiers are
fixed bands of the API list price per million input tokens, each about 3.2× (√10) the last, so
two \$ are 10×: \$ under \$0.32, \$\$ \$0.32 to \$1, \$\$\$ \$1 to \$3.20, \$\$\$\$ \$3.20 to \$10, and \$\$\$\$\$
\$10 and above. Output prices are five times input for all eight models, so the bands hold for
output too. List prices checked 2026-11-06 (input / output): Haiku and Luna \$0.10 / \$0.50, Terra
\$1 / \$5, Sonnet and Sol \$2 / \$10, Opus \$4 / \$20, Fable and Astra \$10 / \$50. The slide shows bands,
not dollars, because the numbers change often; a new price moves only its own model's band.
Subscriptions count usage differently. Haiku's \$ is for prompts up to 100,000 tokens; above that
it costs five times as much (\$\$), which a long session can reach. Which models you can pick depends on your plan and tool
version (Terra needs Codex CLI 0.159.0 or later). Sources, all checked 2026-11-06:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview,
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing,
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config,
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models,
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models. Names and prices change often: re-check this table before
each run. Gemini, used through Antigravity, is not in the table: add it if your group uses it.

📉 The 100–1000× within a few years is our expectation from the trend, not a promise: at a16z's
10× a year, 100× takes about two years and 1,000× about three. The price of a fixed level of
capability has fallen fast: for models matching a given benchmark score, a16z measured about 10×
cheaper each year, 1,000× in the three years from November 2021
([LLMflation](https://a16z.com/llmflation-llm-inference-cost/), Guido Appenzeller, 2024-11-12),
and Epoch AI found 9× to 900× a year depending on the benchmark
([LLM inference price trends](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends),
2025-03-12); both checked 2026-11-07. Both track the cheapest model that reaches a score, not one
model's price list, and both say the pace may slow. Neither measures frontier work, so the
price of what Fable or Astra do today may fall more slowly. The practical point: pick by task,
not by today's price.
:::

## ⌨️ Steer the Assistant: /model · /clear · /exit {#slash-commands}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips style="grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);"}
::: {}
[🧠]{.big}

**`/model`**

bigger + higher effort = more credits · Haiku or Sonnet on **medium**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🧹]{.big}

**`/clear`**

task done? **saves credits** · files stay
:::
::: {.fragment}
[👋]{.big}

**`/exit`** · `/quit`

leave the assistant · type `claude` to return
:::
:::

. . .

💸 **Every reply re-reads the whole chat**: a long conversation costs more tokens each turn

🔁 Next task → `/clear` · 🪫 Prompt keeps failing → `/model`, higher effort · 👋 Done for today → `/exit`

::: {.check}
💬 One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first?
:::

::: {.notes}
Slash commands are typed at the assistant's prompt, not in the shell, and they differ a
little between assistants: `/model` opens a picker for the model and, where the assistant
offers it, the effort (reasoning) level. Higher effort thinks longer: slower and dearer, but
better on multi-step work; medium is enough here. Cost follows tokens, and three things
raise them: a bigger model costs more per token, a higher effort writes more thinking tokens
per reply, and a longer conversation is sent back to the model with every new message, so
each later reply costs more than the first (prompt caching makes repeated context cheaper,
not free, and the cache expires). So the habit is: small model, medium effort, one task per
conversation, `/clear` as soon as a task is done. Plans with usage limits or API credits
drain faster with long chats, big models and high effort; many assistants show usage with a
command or status line (type `/` to look). These cost mechanics are written from general knowledge, not yet checked against each provider's pricing pages or dated: verify before teaching. `/clear` drops the conversation so old
instructions and files read earlier stop steering the assistant and stop using up its
context window; nothing on disk changes, and the project's `AGENTS.md` is read again. Use it
between tasks, and when the assistant seems confused. `/exit` ends the session (`/quit` does
the same in assistants that offer it; Ctrl+C twice or Ctrl+D also leave). Starting it again
in the folder begins a new session, and the files persist. Good answer to the check:
`/clear`, because the new task needs none of the old chat. Type `/` alone to list the
commands of your assistant. Command names written from memory and not yet checked against the official lists
(https://code.claude.com/docs/en/slash-commands, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli):
check them in each assistant (`/` lists them) before teaching, since they change often.
:::

| **medium** | ![Haiku at medium effort: grey-winged pelican on a red bicycle with a proper frame and speed lines.](assets/pelicans/haiku-medium.svg){.pick} [✅ 0.14¢]{.cost} | ![Sonnet at medium effort: white pelican on a thin red bicycle, legs bent towards the pedals, yellow sun.](assets/pelicans/sonnet-medium.svg){.pick} [✅ 1.80¢]{.cost} | ![Opus at medium effort: crested pelican with a large pouch on a red bicycle with a chain ring, yellow sun.](assets/pelicans/opus-medium.svg) [5.89¢]{.cost} | ![Fable at medium effort: white pelican on a red bicycle with black wheels, pale sky.](assets/pelicans/fable-medium.svg) [9.91¢]{.cost} |

: {tbl-colwidths="[8,23,23,23,23]"}

::: {.check}
💬 ✅ is enough here. Is 13¢ worth 90 times a 0.14¢ pelican? · 🕰️ [Every pelican since 2024](https://nilethebot.github.io/pelican-timeline/?ref=runtimewire)
:::

[Images: [Simon Willison's pelican series](https://simonwillison.net/tags/pelican-riding-a-bicycle/), one run per cell ([[Haiku]{translate="no"}](https://gist.github.com/simonw/485dfa24b4efa1267ee2d0911594fb81), [[Sonnet]{translate="no"}](https://gist.github.com/simonw/1d85a9be7f3ecce26e7f1569161a0d01), [[Opus]{translate="no"}](https://gist.github.com/simonw/61fd7c3683fffce9a3ab7c43d1180024), [[Fable]{translate="no"}](https://gist.github.com/simonw/17318f748f8c2b476051ddc2ebeb94a7)) · ¢ = its tokens at API list prices, checked 2026-11-06 · 🌀 [GPT grid](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/openai-pelicans-october-2026.html)]{.source}

::: {.notes}
This makes the previous slide's `/model` choice visible. Read it in two directions. Left to
right is the model: price per token rises, so the cost climbs from fractions of a cent to ten
cents and more. Top to bottom is effort: the assistant thinks longer and writes more, so the
cost usually rises, while the picture often gains details rather than becoming right. Every
cell has a recognisable pelican on a bicycle. Haiku on low has the weakest frame, and from
medium up the frame is right, which is why ✅ medium is the workshop's advice. Stay honest about
the evidence: this is one run per cell of one small, self-contained task, not a benchmark. Run
it again and you get a different bird; Fable's medium even cost less than its low. A drawing
says little about a long job that joins datasets and recovers from errors, which is where
stronger models earn their price. The good answer to the check is "it depends on the task":
for a pelican no, for a hard job that keeps failing perhaps yes, so start small and move up
only when the work needs it. The ratio is 13.09¢ / 0.14¢ = about 93. Costs are for one reply
at API list prices (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing, checked
2026-11-06); a subscription counts usage differently. Both Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 failed at
`max` effort in these runs: they thought for 128,000 tokens and ran out before drawing, so
more is not always better. The Simon Willison series started the prompt
(https://simonwillison.net/tags/pelican-riding-a-bicycle/); the linked timeline, by a third
party, shows how far the drawings have come since 2024. Sources and token counts:
`assets/pelicans/README.md`. No licence is stated on the images: they are credited and linked
here. Nobody needs to run this: it is here to look at.
:::

## 📂 Your Root Folder = The Assistant's World {#root-folder}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[📍]{.big}

**Start it in a folder**

that folder is its **root**: it reads, edits and runs commands there
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🤝]{.big}

**"Trust this folder?"**

answer yes only for a folder you chose for the work
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🚧]{.big}

**Not `~`, not Documents**

a small project folder keeps everything else out of reach
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔄]{.big}

**New project?**

`/exit` · `cd` to its folder · start the assistant again
:::
:::

. . .

🏠 `pwd` before you start: it prints the root

::: {.notes}
When a coding assistant starts it treats the current folder as its root, the default world it
works in: it reads and edits the files there and in the folders below, and runs commands
from there. The first time you start one in a folder it asks whether you trust that folder
(the wording differs between Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity). Trusting it means
you allow the assistant to read the files and, with your approvals, change them and run
commands there, so trust only folders you created for the work, never a folder with other
people's projects, private documents or keys such as `~`, `~/.ssh` or Documents. Project
instructions in the folder, such as `AGENTS.md`, are also read and followed, which is
another reason to trust only your own folders. Starting inside the project folder means
paths in prompts are short (`data/london.csv`), the project's `AGENTS.md` is found, and
a mistake stays inside one folder you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary: approve
each command by reading it, because a command can still name a path outside the root. To
work in another folder, leave with `/exit`, `cd` there and start again. Never run two
assistants writing to one folder. The setup steps use `~/setup` for the install prompt and
each part uses its own project folder. Written from general behaviour of these tools, not
yet checked against each tool's documentation: verify before teaching.
:::

## 📜 Using AI in Research: Say It, Own It {#ai-policy}

[🏠 before the workshop]{.pace} [📖 reading]{.pace}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🚫]{.big}

**Never an author**

AI cannot be accountable
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔍]{.big}

**You verify everything**

code, numbers, references
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔒]{.big}

**Keep private data out**

unpublished or sensitive work stays out of public tools
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📝]{.big}

**Disclose the use**

tool + version · task · your checks
:::
:::

. . .

⚖️ Never generate or alter **primary data or images**: that is misconduct

::: {.check}
💬 Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table? · 📝 [An example](#ai-use-deck)
:::

::: {.notes}
Publishers' policies differ, so read the one for your journal, course or employer before
submitting. The common core, from the summary supplied for this deck (not yet checked
against each publisher's own policy page: do that before teaching, and record the date):
AI tools are not listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility; the authors
verify AI output, including facts and references, and answer for plagiarism; unpublished
manuscripts, review reports, participant data and proprietary work are not uploaded to
public AI tools. Where to disclose depends on the use. Basic copyediting (grammar, spelling)
is usually exempt. Drafting or translating text goes in the acknowledgements or a
declaration, with the tool and version. Data analysis and coding go in the Methods, with
enough detail to reproduce them. Explanatory diagrams are disclosed in the caption or
declaration. Generating or altering primary research images or raw data is prohibited.
Other common forms, from the same summary: for translation, name the tool and say you reviewed
the translated sections so the meaning was preserved; for a diagram made with a generative
tool, say which figure, which tool and version, that you edited and labelled it, and that it
fabricates no primary data; and, optionally, a statement that no AI tools were used.
Publishers also differ in form: some ask for a separate AI declaration with the submission,
some for a note in the cover letter, and some ban AI-generated images outright. This
workshop is a reason to practise: you direct an assistant, so you will have something to
disclose. The 📝 link opens this deck's own statement, its second slide: adapt it by naming
your own assistant and model exactly as your assistant names them, with the version, saying
which tasks it performed, and keeping the last sentence. Good answer to the check: a typo fix
is basic copyediting and is usually exempt; computing a table is analysis and belongs in the
Methods, with enough detail to reproduce it, which here is the code and the `AGENTS.md` that
the project keeps.
:::

## 🧰 Three Boxes, Three Roles {#three-boxes}

[👀 An example: you will paste prompts like this from Part 1 on.]{.source}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and one welcome paragraph.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `london.md` · may run `quarto render london.md`
:::

::: {.you}
approve its commands · open `london.html` in your browser
:::

::: {.notes}
Violet: paste this prompt into your coding assistant (use the copy button).
Amber: what the assistant will probably run; you do not repeat it. Green: the few
things you type or click yourself, such as accounts, publishing and opening files. The
assistant occupies its terminal, so type green commands (such as `quarto preview`) in a
second terminal tab opened in the same folder.
The prompts are examples, not transcripts: assistants vary, so check the result.
:::

## 🧪 Prompts Are Engineered · 🔍 Ask When Unsure {#prompts-engineered}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🧪]{.big}

**Engineered prompts**

designed with AI to reduce errors
:::
::: {}
[❓]{.big}

**Don't understand it?**

ask an AI or search the docs
:::
::: {}
[🔍]{.big}

**Dig deeper**

what it does, why, when to use it
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.prompt}
```default
Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.
```
:::

::: {.notes}
The prompts in this deck were written with AI assistance and refined to reduce the chance
of errors, but they are not magic and assistants vary. Whenever a concept, option or command
is unfamiliar (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), do not just paste and move
on: ask your assistant, or read the official documentation, to understand what it does,
why it is used and where else it applies. Understanding the details lets you spot when a
result is wrong and adapt the prompts to your own work. The prompt above is an example of
such a question; use it on any term in the deck.
:::

## 🗣️ How to Prompt Your Coding Assistant {#how-to-prompt}

::: {.cards .tips}
::: {}
[🎯]{.big}

**Be specific**

file names, columns, chart types
:::
::: {}
[☝️]{.big}

**One step at a time**

one task per prompt
:::
::: {}
[✅]{.big}

**Ask it to run & check**

"…render it and tell me about errors"
:::
::: {}
[👀]{.big}

**Check what changed**

you are responsible for the result
:::
:::

🌍 ¿Español? Your first prompt can be: `Responde siempre en español; deja el código y los nombres de archivo en inglés.`

::: {.notes}
A good prompt names the file, the content, the output and a completion check. Browser
translation translates the prompts on the slides, and the copy button copies the
translation; the file names, columns, options and commands in them stay in English, so
the assistant still finds them. You may also write your own prompts in Spanish.
Short follow-ups work once the conversation has context. Ask the assistant to show
what it changed; read the diff before moving on.
:::
